questions.q: Per this lesson's extraction process, where should you look for essential parameter values beyond the main body text?
options: Figure captions, table footnotes, and the appendix/supplementary material
Only the paper's title and abstract
The journal's editorial policy page
The paper's acknowledgments section
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly lists checking every figure caption and table footnote, plus the appendix/supplementary material, as essential steps because papers routinely put parameter values there.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend writing your own methodology document, in your own words, before writing any code?
options: Translating the paper's description into your own words reveals what you don't yet understand, before it costs debugging time
Because journals require a separate methodology document for publication
Because code cannot be written until a paper is formally cited
Because writing a document is faster than building the actual circuit
questions.explain: The lesson states this step matters because translating the paper's description into your own words surfaces gaps in your understanding early, before they turn into debugging problems.

questions.q: How does the lesson say you should treat a detail like the exact random seed used for a stochastic optimizer, when the paper's claim is about average convergence behavior?
options: As a detail that plausibly doesn't affect the qualitative result -- reasonable to choose yourself and document
As a fatal gap that makes the paper impossible to reproduce at all
As something that must be guessed silently with no documentation
As evidence the original paper is fraudulent
questions.explain: The lesson distinguishes details that plausibly don't affect the qualitative result (like a random seed for average-behavior claims) from details that do -- the former is reasonable to choose yourself and document, not something to treat as a fatal flaw.

questions.q: In the worked GHZ/zero-noise-extrapolation example, why couldn't the methodology be fully extracted from the paper's own methods section alone?
options: The paper said it used 'the technique of [citation]' for the folding method, requiring the cited paper to confirm exactly how folding was implemented
The paper provided no information about the circuit at all
The paper never mentioned shot counts anywhere, including captions
The paper's appendix was entirely blank
questions.explain: The worked example shows the main paper cites an external technique for unitary folding without fully re-specifying it, meaning the cited prior work needs to be consulted to complete the methodology -- a normal, reasonable practice the lesson describes.

questions.q: According to the lesson, how should a specification gap that plausibly DOES affect the result (e.g., which error-mitigation sub-technique was used, among several variants) be handled?
options: Flagged explicitly, not silently guessed around, because it affects how any later discrepancy should be interpreted
Ignored, since all error-mitigation variants produce identical results
Resolved by abandoning the reproduction attempt entirely
Silently filled in with any convenient choice and never mentioned again
questions.explain: The lesson draws a clear line: gaps that could plausibly change the result must be flagged explicitly, because they directly affect how you'd interpret a later discrepancy between your result and the paper's, which Lesson 9 covers in depth.
